---
title: "Ruby for non-Rubyists"
---

Everything needed to read the code in this book, assuming you program in
something else. Sonic Pi is Ruby with a music DSL on top, and this book uses a
small corner of the language.

## Symbols

`:c4` is a symbol: an interned string used as a name. Sonic Pi uses them for
note names, synth names, and scale names.

```ruby
play :c4          # symbol
play 60           # the same note as an integer
```

Symbols are values, so they work as hash keys and array members. `:c4 + 12`
also works inside Sonic Pi because its music layer converts note symbols during
arithmetic. Plain Ruby does not give arbitrary symbols that behaviour.

## Arrays and indexing

Arrays use zero-based indexes, negative indexes count from the end, and a range
selects a slice.

```ruby
notes = [60, 62, 64, 65]
notes[0]       # => 60
notes[-1]      # => 65
notes[1..2]    # => [62, 64]
```

`+` joins arrays and `rotate` moves values from the front to the back. The scale
and mode chapters use both. Methods with a trailing `!` usually mutate their
receiver; this book prefers the non-mutating form when score data is involved.

```ruby
[60, 64] + [67]          # => [60, 64, 67]
[0, 2, 4, 5].rotate(1)  # => [2, 4, 5, 0]
```

## Hashes and event data

A hash maps keys to values. The event schema uses symbols as keys. Modern Ruby
allows `note: 60` as shorthand for `:note => 60`.

```ruby
event = {note: 60, start: 0, duration: 1, amp: 0.8}
event[:note]            # => 60
event.fetch(:duration)  # => 1
event.fetch(:pan, 0)    # => 0 when :pan is absent
```

`fetch` is useful when absence is an error or when a default should be visible.
Square-bracket lookup returns `nil` for a missing key, which can hide a spelling
mistake until the renderer runs.

## Blocks

A block is an anonymous function passed to a method, written with `do ... end`
or braces. Parameters go between vertical bars.

```ruby
4.times do |i|
  play 60 + i
  sleep 0.5
end
```

## each and map

`each` iterates for effect. `map` transforms and returns a new array. Both take
blocks.

```ruby
[60, 64, 67].each { |n| play n; sleep 0.5 }
[60, 64, 67].map  { |n| n + 12 }              # => [72, 76, 79]
```

Destructuring works in block parameters, which is how the score walker reads
pairs:

```ruby
[[:c4, 1], [:e4, 0.5]].each do |pitch, duration|
  play pitch
  sleep duration
end
```

Several nearby methods appear in later lessons:

```ruby
[60, 62, 64].each_cons(2).to_a  # => [[60, 62], [62, 64]]
[60, 64, 67].zip([1, 1, 2])     # => [[60, 1], [64, 1], [67, 2]]
[1, 2, 3].sum                    # => 6
```

`each_cons(2)` exposes adjacent values, which suits interval and voice-leading
checks. `zip` aligns parallel arrays by index. `sum` is used for bar-duration
assertions.

## Conditions

Ruby's `if` is an expression, and a short condition can follow the statement it
controls.

```ruby
quality = interval == 4 ? :major : :minor
play note if note

if duration <= 0
  raise "duration must be positive"
end
```

Only `false` and `nil` are false in Ruby. Zero is true. That difference matters
when pitch class 0 represents C.

`case` works well for symbolic music data:

```ruby
offsets = case quality
          when :major then [0, 4, 7]
          when :minor then [0, 3, 7]
          else raise "unknown quality"
          end
```

## Keyword arguments

Trailing `name: value` pairs. Sonic Pi uses them for everything expressive.

```ruby
play :c4, amp: 0.7, release: 2, cutoff: 90
```

## Defining functions

Sonic Pi wraps `def` in `define`, which registers the function with the runtime
so it survives across runs and is available inside threads.

```ruby
define :play_phrase do |score, transpose: 0|
  score.each { |pitch, duration| play pitch + transpose; sleep duration }
end
```

Arguments before the keyword section are positional. A keyword with a default is
optional; one without a default is required. The final expression becomes the
return value.

```ruby
define :transpose do |notes, by:|
  notes.map { |n| n + by }
end

transpose([60, 64, 67], by: 12)
```

Keep definitions above their first call in a fresh buffer. Sonic Pi remembers a
named definition across runs, but examples in this book never depend on that
history.

## Rings

A ring is Sonic Pi's own type: an array whose index wraps. `ring(1, 2, 3)[4]`
returns `2`. Useful for patterns that outlive the sequence they are drawn from.

```ruby
notes = ring(:c4, :e4, :g4)
8.times { |i| play notes[i]; sleep 0.5 }   # cycles, no bounds error
```

Sonic Pi adds `tick` and `look` for counters associated with the current thread.
`tick` advances and returns the counter; `look` reads it without advancing.

```ruby
notes = ring(:c4, :e4, :g4)
6.times do
  play notes.tick
  sleep 0.5
end
```

An explicit loop index is easier to inspect when several rings must advance at
different rates. The book uses `tick` for repeating performance patterns and an
index for transformations whose positions carry meaning.

## Numeric details

Pitch arithmetic uses integers. Beat durations often use floats, because Ruby
2.6 evaluates `2 / 3` as integer division while `2.0 / 3` keeps the fraction.
Modulo wraps pitch classes and pattern indexes.

```ruby
61 % 12       # => 1, the pitch class C-sharp or D-flat
2.0 / 3       # => 0.6666666666666666
13 % 4        # => 1, the second slot in a four-step pattern
```

Floating-point duration sums can carry tiny rounding errors. A check over many
fractional events should compare within a tolerance instead of demanding exact
equality.

## Threads and shared state

`in_thread` and `live_loop` run blocks concurrently under Sonic Pi's deterministic
scheduler. Local variables are captured when a thread begins, but coordination
between long-lived loops uses `cue` and `sync`. Sonic Pi also provides `set` and
`get` for named state.

Prefer messages and immutable score data to shared mutable arrays. A live loop
that reads a changing array while another loop writes it is harder to reason
about than two loops starting from the same cue and reading stable data.

## Things that trip you up

Ruby returns the last expression, so functions rarely need `return`. Integer
division truncates, so write `2.0/3` and not `2/3` when you mean a triplet.
Symbols and strings are different types, and Sonic Pi wants symbols. Method names
may end in `?` without changing call syntax; the punctuation signals a Boolean
result by convention.
